entries.text: Ramesh’s absence renders the kitchen a dead letter; there is no food to be had here, only the cold silence of an empty larder. I must abandon the notion of a domestic breakfast and face the reality that my sustenance must be procured in the public sphere, even if it means waiting for the sun to be higher. The body is a stubborn fact, but it is not the master.
A watchman at the gate of the next bungalow crouches over a small fire of dry leaves and twigs, a grey blanket round his shoulders and his hands held out to the smoke.

The watchman crouches by his leaf-fire, hands out to the smoke, a small ritual of warmth against the December chill. It is a private act, yet it marks the boundary of the estate, a human sentinel holding the line between my bungalow and the rest of the world. I note the contrast: I am indoors, dry and safe, while he is exposed, yet his stillness has a dignity that my own hurried plans lack.

Shri Hegde stands in the doorway, the man whose name was mistaken for mine by the Directorate. I must address him before he leaves, for the absurdity of my tenure rests entirely on his absence. I will ask him plainly if he requires this bungalow, knowing that his refusal to correct the record is the only thing keeping me here.
Shri Hegde, I am told you are the intended occupant of this residence. I am here only by a clerical error. Do you wish to claim it, or shall I remain the ghost in the machine?
Sir, I am the occupant, yes, but I am also the man who has to file the complaint. If you are the ghost, please sign the intake form and let me go, I have a hearing at twelve.

He is treating me as an obstruction, a bureaucratic error to be filed away. I will not be the ghost in his machine. I must clarify the absurdity of his premise: I am not the ghost; I am the man who woke up in his body, or rather, in the body the state assigned to me. But he is in a hurry. I will give him the signature he seeks, not to dismiss him, but to end the confusion. It is a small act of formal decision, the dot upon the i.

Shri Hegde, you are not filing a complaint against a ghost. You are filing a correction against a clerical error that has become ontological. I will sign your form. But understand: I am not leaving. I am the one who remains. The Directorate has confused the names, but it has not confused the flesh. I am here. You are here. The state is here. Let us sort the paper, and then let us go our separate ways, you to your hearing, and I to my museum.
Museum? Sir, this is a government bungalow, not a gallery. You are making a mess of a simple administrative error. Sign the paper here, in the blue box, and stop talking about flesh and ontology.

He is a man of the department, and to him a signature is the end of a sentence. I see the tension: he wants to close the file, but I am the content of the file. To sign is to accept the premise of the error, to make myself a thing to be moved. I will not sign. I will sit, and let the silence do the work of the concept.

Shri Hegde, I see the urgency of your pen, but I cannot sign what I am not. I am not Shri G. Hegde. To sign would be to deny my own existence, and that is a contradiction I do not intend to enter into. I will wait for the Directorate to resolve the identity, not for me to erase it.

Sir, I don't have time to debate your existence with you. I have a hearing in under two hours and the clerk is already staring at me. If you won't sign, I'm leaving this form unsigned and telling the Directorate you're obstructing official business.

Her impatience is the blunt instrument of bureaucracy: to her, the anomaly is a line to be struck through, not a contradiction to be resolved. I am not a clerk, nor am I an obstruction, though I am neither. I will not sign a lie, but I will not be the cause of her trouble either; the form is her responsibility, not mine. She is leaving, and I am hungry; the museum can wait for a man who is not starving.

Shri Hegde, I will not sign a form that misstates the facts of my occupancy, nor will I be the cause of your dismissal. Take the form. I am a guest of the state, not its enemy. You may tell the Directorate what you like; I shall be here when the truth is required.

You think you are the state? The state is the file, sir, and the file says Hegde. I am not going to get dismissed for your philosophical hobby; if you won't sign, I am leaving this unsigned and telling the Directorate you are obstructing official business. Good day.

She has left, and with her the last pretence of a dialogue. I had expected a clerk to obey, or a man to argue; instead, I have been threatened by a woman who mistakes her stamp for the soul of the state. It is a grotesque inversion, but I shall not chase her. I must go to the Museum, as planned, to see the stone that outlasts the ink.

The file note lingers, but the museum is open until six, and I have a full morning before lunch. I shall go straight to the galleries of the subcontinent; the artifacts speak of a spirit that dreams, and I must see with my own eyes what I have only read about in the lecture notes.

The donors stand in rigid rows, their faces erased by time but their posture still bearing the weight of hierarchical submission. It is the same spirit as the caste system: the individual dissolved into the universal, yet a universal that is merely natural, not free. I see the tension between the artistic expression of devotion and the political stasis it implies.

A Pahari miniature: Radha and Krishna sharing a single cloak against the storm, the lightning rendered as a gold thread. Here is the individual will, the particular feeling, elevated into art. It is not the fixed, substantial caste hierarchy of the text I carry, but the subjective spirit expressing itself in beauty. Yet it remains within the bounds of the particular; it does not yet reach the universal ethical substance of the state, but it is a free movement of the soul within a limited sphere.

The rudra veena, with its two gourds, stands silent behind the glass, a relic of a devotion I cannot hear but can see in its rigid structure. It is a beautiful object, yet it remains a thing, a mere instrument of a spirit that dreams rather than acts. I have spent enough time with these artifacts; the hunger of sixteen hours ago is becoming a physical demand that supersedes my curiosity.

The walk from the museum has cooled me, but the hunger in my stomach is a practical matter that cannot be resolved by philosophy alone. The IIC is open, and the plan calls for lunch here to observe the civil society of the club. I shall not waste the hour; the guard is merely a sentinel, and the officer is likely occupied with his own duties. I will seek the dining hall.

The hunger has passed, but the afternoon stretches out with a clarity that is almost aggressive. I am seated in the IIC, watching the civil society of the club operate with its own quiet logic, while the file in my pocket—a letter from Shri Malhotra—reminds me that I am still an object of curiosity, or perhaps concern, to the state. I must not let the dream of this place consume me; I am a man of the Germanic world, even if I sleep in a bungalow meant for a Joint Secretary.
The pond in the garden is half covered with the round leaves of water lilies, and sparrows drink from the stone edge where the water has dropped.

The pond sits like a mirror cracked by the lilies, a stillness that mocks the sparrows' frantic thirst. I am tired, and the plan for the afternoon walk to Safdarjung is still before me, but the body insists on rest before it can contemplate the tombs. I shall sit here in the shade and let the heat of the midday pass.

The hunger returns with the persistence of a bad argument; the library offers only silence, not sustenance. I shall walk to Khan Market, where the system of needs is open and indifferent to my philosophical contemplations, and satisfy this biological imperative.

entries.text: At the State Bank branch in Khan Market the clerk offers to open a savings account against Mr. Saxena's letter.
He declines: not today.

The State Bank clerk offers to open a savings account with Mr. Saxena's letter. I have no bank account, only a cheque that is currently useless paper. To make the system of needs work for me, I must first have a place to deposit the universal credit. I will speak to the clerk now.

Mr. Clerk, you mention that with Mr. Saxena's letter I may open a savings account today. Please, I would like to proceed. I have a cheque for ten thousand rupees that I wish to deposit once the account is established.
I am not the clerk, and I do not do banking. Go to the bank, Masterji has a shop to close.

Masterji is right; I was confusing the clerk with the tailor in my hunger and haste. The bank clerk stands there, but it is half past three, and the light is beginning to thin. I have no use for a savings account today; I have cash, and I have a recital to attend. I will take a cup of chai to steady my nerves and then walk to the Habitat Centre.
You are correct, Masterji. My apologies. I will take my leave.
Save your apologies for the bank manager. Go.

The tailor’s command is sharp and correct; I have lingered too long in civil society’s chatter when the tombs await. The sun is still high, and the heat is manageable at this hour, but the light will fail soon. I must move to Safdarjung before the shadows swallow the domes.
You are right, Masterji. The hour is against me. I go.
Door is open. Don't forget your kurta.

The gate is closing in three minutes, and I have only bought the right to enter, not the time to see. The haze has swallowed the details of the dome, and the clerk’s eyes are already on the clock. I am a foreigner here, in the literal and the philosophical sense; I must pay the price of admission to see what is actually present, not what I imagine to be there.
One entry ticket, please. I am a foreign visitor.
Three hundred rupees, sir. The gate shuts at 5:24, so you’ve got just over two hours to see it all.

Two hours is ample time to walk the perimeter and observe the tomb, though the heat of the afternoon sun has already begun to fade. I have paid the price of admission; now I must claim the experience. The clerk’s urgency is that of a man who values time over substance, but I intend to let the stone speak to me at its own pace.
Thank you. I shall make the best of the remaining light.
The light is decent, yes. The tomb dome catches it nicely this time of day, so take your time with the photography.

Sixteen minutes. The clerk suggests I take my time, but the gate does not care for photography. I have seen the dome under the haze; the light is better now, but I am not a tourist. I will step inside, look at the play of shadow on the marble one last time, and leave before they lock the doors and I am trapped in a courtyard with no key.
The light is indeed better, though the gate does not wait for the lens. I will finish my circuit.
Yeah, the gate doesn't wait, but you've got fifteen minutes left, sir. Hurry up a little if you want to get the last shots before the lights come on.

The hunger is a sharp reminder that the body demands satisfaction before the mind can contemplate. I see Mrs. Kapoor; a retired schoolteacher is a figure of the ethical order, someone who has spent a life in the discipline of the school. I shall purchase a simple meal here to sustain myself, as the stall offers, and perhaps engage her in brief conversation regarding the nature of duty.
Good evening, Madam. The air is pleasant. I find myself in need of sustenance; might I trouble you for a moment's conversation while I eat?
You say 'sustenance' like it's a word from a textbook, not a tummy that's growling. Sit down, I'm not going anywhere until the sun sets.

The old lady is right to be blunt; my stomach has been grumbling since the corn, and I have walked far enough for my legs to ache. I have no business being here in the evening, having missed the sitar recital I had planned. I will sit with her for a moment, accept the hospitality of the hour, and then make for home before the dark takes the gardens.

You are correct, Madam. The body is a fact that resists philosophy. I am exhausted from my walk and have missed my evening plans. I shall sit with you until the light fails, and then I must go. Tell me, do you know of any shop that sells a decent bottle of wine in this part of the city?
Wine? Pah, you look like a ghost already. There's a liquor store two lanes down near the gate, but I won't be your guide to the bottle. Just eat your corn and let the silence do its work.

Mrs. Kapoor’s refusal to guide me to the bottle is a small but telling act of moral authority; she sees the ghost in me and names it. I have eaten the corn and the water, and the silence she prescribes is not empty but full of the day’s accumulated observations. It is time to leave the garden before the light fails completely and to return to the bungalow to rest.

entries.text: You are right, Mrs. Kapoor. The silence is sufficient. Thank you for your honesty.
Don't thank me, just thank the corn. I'm not a saint, I'm a retired woman who likes to watch the light change on the water. Sit still and eat.

The walk has taken its toll; my legs ache and the house offers the only quiet I can claim. I shall sit by the window and let the evening settle over the day's events, particularly the strange tension in Malhotra's letter and the way my own certainties have shifted under the weight of what I have seen.

It is a strange, cheerful intrusion into the evening quiet, a reminder that the city does not sleep but merely changes its noise. I am too tired to walk, and the food situation remains dire, so I will stay put and let the sound pass.

entries.text: The hunger is a physical fact that demands a universal resolution: food. Ramesh is absent, so the household cannot provide, and the file on my desk is a bureaucratic abstraction that will not feed me. Hegde is still there, likely waiting for a signature or a decision, but my body requires sustenance before I can engage with the state's paperwork. I must address the immediate need before the abstract one.

Hegde, before we proceed with the file, I require a meal. I have not eaten since yesterday evening, and the household cook is absent. Do you know a place nearby that is open and serves a simple dinner? I will pay in cash.

Sir, it’s nearly eight, most places are winding down. There’s a small dhaba right behind the bungalow compound, the one with the blue tarpaulin; they usually keep the tandoor hot till ten. I’ll walk you there if you like, or I can call ahead so they don't make you wait.

The man has offered a path to the tandoor, and the hunger in my belly has turned from a private affliction into a matter of logistical coordination. I am no longer merely a man who is hungry; I am a guest in a system of needs that Hegde, as the agent of the state, is now managing for me. The irony is not lost on me: the state provides the food, even if it refuses the name.
Thank you, Shri Hegde. I will accept your escort. The tandoor sounds preferable to the silence of an empty house. Please, lead the way.
After you, sir. Just watch your step on the gatepost, it’s a bit loose. I’ll get us two rotis and some dal, or whatever they have left.

The man is gone, leaving me to navigate the physical world with the caution of a guest who knows he is not the master. The loose gatepost is a minor hazard, but the promise of food is a universal necessity that overrides my pride. I will follow him, keeping my eyes on the path and my dignity intact, for a body that is not fed cannot contemplate the Absolute.

entries.text: I shall follow, Shri Hegde. Do take care yourself; the dark is already falling.
Don't worry, sir, I've walked this path a hundred times. Just keep your eyes on the ground and we'll be there in two minutes.

He speaks with the confidence of a man who has walked this path a hundred times, yet his hand hovers near the gatepost as if the ground itself might betray us. It is a small, practical wisdom that I, with all my lectures on the actuality of the state, have not yet mastered: the knowledge of the immediate, physical step. I will follow his lead, keeping my eyes on the uneven earth rather than the stars.
Thank you, Shri Hegde. Your caution is noted; I shall attend to the ground.
Ara, don't be so formal. Just walk, sir. The food will get cold if we stand here talking.

The Joint Secretary yields to the practical necessity of a cold meal, abandoning his threat of dismissal for the time being. It is a small concession, but it confirms that the file, for all its bureaucratic rigidity, cannot yet swallow the living man who occupies the space. I will follow him to the table, for the hunger is real, and the evening is too short to argue with a man who is merely hungry.
You are right. The body has its own dialectic. I shall follow.
Dialectic? You've got a strange one for a dinner guest. Keep up, the dal is waiting.

The engine notes what the body already knows: there is nothing to eat. Ramesh is gone, and the kitchen is silent. Hegde’s invitation to dinner is a phantom, a bureaucratic ghost refusing to dissolve. I will not play at hunger that cannot be satisfied. I will sit, and perhaps open a book, while he waits for a meal that does not exist.
The dal is a fiction, Shri Hegde. As is your file. I shall sit, and you may wait for the imaginary meal as long as you like.
Beta, the dal is real, I made it myself this afternoon. It’s not a philosophy exam, just dinner. Sit down before I start the lecture.

The threat of the file dissolves in the steam of a pot of dal. Here is the state made flesh: not the abstract ethical idea, but a man who cooks for his subordinate to keep the peace. I am hungry, and the practical necessity of the body overrides my philosophical pride. I will sit, for the moment, where the file has placed me.

shelf.ref: The Historical Side of This Connection

entries.text: The file may say Hegde, but the stomach says Hegel. I accept the hospitality, though I note that the state is currently running on lentils and patience.
Arre, stop with the fancy words and just eat before the dal gets cold. You are running on lentils and patience, but at least the lentils are hot.

shelf_exposure.text: It is the artist within, who shapes and forms the material without. From within the root or the seed-grain it makes the shoot come forth; from this again it brings the branches, and from them the twigs, and from out of the twigs it calls forth the buds, and leaves, and flowers. All is planned, prepared and perfected within.

Now amongst these some have an equal part in common; fire and water, for example, have warmth; thus if in fire dryness were overcome by moisture, out of fire air would arise. On the contrary, as regards those which have nothing in common with one another, like earth, which is cold and dry, and air, which is warm and moist, the transition goes more slowly forward.

shelf_exposure.text: We may therefore state the first point in Kant's philosophy as follows: Thought must itself investigate its own capacity of knowledge. I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

You ask if the glacier has moved. I can report that it has, though not as dramatically as you might hope. The file of Shri G. Hegde remains in its purgatory, but I have received a letter from Shri R. K. Malhotra, an IAS officer retired. He writes to inform me that he knows the occupant. It is a strange thing, to be known by a man whose name appears only in the carbon copies of the Directorate. He does not ask for my name; he asks for the occupant’s. The distinction is not merely semantic; it is ontological. I am the occupant, but I am not the name. The state requires the name to function, but I exist in the gap between the two. I am the grain in the machine, and the machine grinds on, indifferent to the shape of the grain.

You mention the grey, wet fog of Munich. Here, the air is sharp today, a rare clarity that felt like a gift from a god who had finally decided to look. The haze lifted, and for the first time in weeks, I could see the domes of the Lodis in Lodhi Gardens, standing in the clear air like thoughts that have not yet been dismissed. It was a beautiful sight, and a melancholy one. The tombs are the conquerors’ work, built by those who took this land in turn. A country taken by everyone has a history the way a road has traffic. I walked among them, and I thought of your boy writing about justice in the Republic. Justice, too, is a road that has traffic. It moves, but it does not stop. It does not look back.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal. I have been revising my notes on the Ethical Substance. I find that my old convictions are being shaken, not by the events of my life here, but by the very nature of the place. India is not merely outside world history; it is a different kind of history, one that does not fit into my previous categories. I am learning to see it anew, and it is a humbling experience. The state is not the dream; it is the machine. And the machine grinds. I am the grain. But perhaps, in the grinding, something new is being made.

With warm regards,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

Dear Dr. Lindner,

The air has cleared for the second day in a row, a crisp, cold clarity that feels less like a mercy and more like a judgment. It is the kind of evening that demands one sit up straight, for the shadows are sharp and the silence is audible. I have just finished my dinner, a modest affair, and Ramesh, the caretaker, has retreated to the gatehouse. In his quiet efficiency, in the way he leaves a warm plate without a word and respects the boundary of my study, I find the ethical substance you spoke of. It is not in the grand declarations of the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions that hold the household together. It is a truth that humbles my old lectures on the Absolute.

The file of Shri Hegde remains in its purgatory, but a new element has entered the scene. I received a letter today from Shri R. K. Malhotra, an IAS officer retired. He writes to inform me that he knows the occupant. It is a strange thing, to be known by a man whose name appears only in the carbon copies of the Directorate. I do not know if this will lead to my expulsion or my absorption, but I know that the universal claim of the administration is beginning to recognize the particular will of the ghost in the bungalow.

I have been walking in the evenings, a habit I have taken up to clear the head. The city at night is a different creature from the city in the haze. The lights are sharper, the sounds more distinct. records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, I am told you are the intended occupant of this residence. I am here only by a clerical error. Do you wish to claim it, or shall I remain the ghost in the machine?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, I am the occupant, yes, but I am also the man who has to file the complaint. If you are the ghost, please sign the intake form and let me go, I have a hearing at twelve.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, you are not filing a complaint against a ghost. You are filing a correction against a clerical error that has become ontological. I will sign your form. But understand: I am not leaving. I am the one who remains. The Directorate has confused the names, but it has not confused the flesh. I am here. You are here. The state is here. Let us sort the paper, and then let us go our separate ways, you to your hearing, and I to my museum.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Museum? Sir, this is a government bungalow, not a gallery. You are making a mess of a simple administrative error. Sign the paper here, in the blue box, and stop talking about flesh and ontology.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, I see the urgency of your pen, but I cannot sign what I am not. I am not Shri G. Hegde. To sign would be to deny my own existence, and that is a contradiction I do not intend to enter into. I will wait for the Directorate to resolve the identity, not for me to erase it.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, I don't have time to debate your existence with you. I have a hearing in under two hours and the clerk is already staring at me. If you won't sign, I'm leaving this form unsigned and telling the Directorate you're obstructing official business.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, I will not sign a form that misstates the facts of my occupancy, nor will I be the cause of your dismissal. Take the form. I am a guest of the state, not its enemy. You may tell the Directorate what you like; I shall be here when the truth is required.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: You think you are the state? The state is the file, sir, and the file says Hegde. I am not going to get dismissed for your philosophical hobby; if you won't sign, I am leaving this unsigned and telling the Directorate you are obstructing official business. Good day.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Clerk, you mention that with Mr. Saxena's letter I may open a savings account today. Please, I would like to proceed. I have a cheque for ten thousand rupees that I wish to deposit once the account is established.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: I am not the clerk, and I do not do banking. Go to the bank, Masterji has a shop to close.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Masterji. My apologies. I will take my leave.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Save your apologies for the bank manager. Go.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Masterji. The hour is against me. I go.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Door is open. Don't forget your kurta.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: One entry ticket, please. I am a foreign visitor.

records.speaker: The ticket clerk
records.words: Three hundred rupees, sir. The gate shuts at 5:24, so you’ve got just over two hours to see it all.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you. I shall make the best of the remaining light.

records.speaker: The ticket clerk
records.words: The light is decent, yes. The tomb dome catches it nicely this time of day, so take your time with the photography.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The light is indeed better, though the gate does not wait for the lens. I will finish my circuit.

records.speaker: The ticket clerk
records.words: Yeah, the gate doesn't wait, but you've got fifteen minutes left, sir. Hurry up a little if you want to get the last shots before the lights come on.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good evening, Madam. The air is pleasant. I find myself in need of sustenance; might I trouble you for a moment's conversation while I eat?

records.speaker: Mrs. Kapoor
records.words: You say 'sustenance' like it's a word from a textbook, not a tummy that's growling. Sit down, I'm not going anywhere until the sun sets.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Madam. The body is a fact that resists philosophy. I am exhausted from my walk and have missed my evening plans. I shall sit with you until the light fails, and then I must go. Tell me, do you know of any shop that sells a decent bottle of wine in this part of the city?

records.speaker: Mrs. Kapoor
records.words: Wine? Pah, you look like a ghost already. There's a liquor store two lanes down near the gate, but I won't be your guide to the bottle. Just eat your corn and let the silence do its work.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Mrs. Kapoor. The silence is sufficient. Thank you for your honesty.

records.speaker: Mrs. Kapoor
records.words: Don't thank me, just thank the corn. I'm not a saint, I'm a retired woman who likes to watch the light change on the water. Sit still and eat.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Hegde, before we proceed with the file, I require a meal. I have not eaten since yesterday evening, and the household cook is absent. Do you know a place nearby that is open and serves a simple dinner? I will pay in cash.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, it’s nearly eight, most places are winding down. There’s a small dhaba right behind the bungalow compound, the one with the blue tarpaulin; they usually keep the tandoor hot till ten. I’ll walk you there if you like, or I can call ahead so they don't make you wait.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Shri Hegde. I will accept your escort. The tandoor sounds preferable to the silence of an empty house. Please, lead the way.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: After you, sir. Just watch your step on the gatepost, it’s a bit loose. I’ll get us two rotis and some dal, or whatever they have left.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I shall follow, Shri Hegde. Do take care yourself; the dark is already falling.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Don't worry, sir, I've walked this path a hundred times. Just keep your eyes on the ground and we'll be there in two minutes.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Shri Hegde. Your caution is noted; I shall attend to the ground.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Ara, don't be so formal. Just walk, sir. The food will get cold if we stand here talking.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right. The body has its own dialectic. I shall follow.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Dialectic? You've got a strange one for a dinner guest. Keep up, the dal is waiting.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The dal is a fiction, Shri Hegde. As is your file. I shall sit, and you may wait for the imaginary meal as long as you like.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Beta, the dal is real, I made it myself this afternoon. It’s not a philosophy exam, just dinner. Sit down before I start the lecture.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The file may say Hegde, but the stomach says Hegel. I accept the hospitality, though I note that the state is currently running on lentils and patience.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Arre, stop with the fancy words and just eat before the dal gets cold. You are running on lentils and patience, but at least the lentils are hot.
